title: Missing Number
statement: An array nums contains n distinct numbers drawn from the range [0, n] — that is, n + 1 candidate values with exactly one of them absent. Return the missing number, ideally in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
realWorld: Finding the one sequence number a consumer never acknowledged. A producer stamps messages 0..n, the sink reports back which ids it durably stored, and the gap has to be located without sorting the list or building a set the size of the stream — which is the whole point when the ids number in the millions.

examples.explanation: n = 3, so the candidates are 0,1,2,3. Every one of them appears except 2.
n = 2, so the candidates are 0,1,2 and the missing value is n itself. This is the case that breaks every solution that only ever looks at indices 0..n-1.
Order tells you nothing here — the answer has to come from an aggregate over the whole array, not from a position.

constraints: All values in nums are distinct, and exactly one value from [0, n] is missing

bruteForce.idea: For every candidate value from 0 to n, scan the array to see whether it is present; return the first one that is not.
bruteForce.whySlow: n + 1 candidates each trigger a full scan, and every scan walks past the same values the previous scan has already rejected. The array is read n times end to end to extract a single fact — which of the n + 1 values never appears — and that fact is an aggregate one pass could have accumulated. Sorting first is the same trade in a nicer wrapper: n log n comparisons to establish an order the answer does not depend on.

patternIdentification: The input is a known, closed set with one element removed. That means you never have to search for the absentee: compare the whole input against what a complete set would look like, using an aggregate where everything present cancels out. XOR cancels because a ^ a == 0 and a ^ 0 == a; sums cancel because the complete total has the closed form n(n+1)/2. The same move solves 'find the duplicate', 'find the element that appears once', and 'find the two swapped values'.

optimized.idea: XOR every index together with every value. Each present value v sits at some index and also appears as a candidate index somewhere in 0..n, so it is XORed an even number of times and cancels to 0; the missing value appears only as an index and survives. Seed the accumulator with n, since the index n has no nums[n] to pair with. The sum formula n(n+1)/2 - sum(nums) is the other classic answer and is just as short, but its accumulator can overflow for large n while XOR never can, because every intermediate value stays inside the same bit width as the inputs.
code: int missing = n;                // index n exists as a candidate but has no element
missing ^= i ^ nums[i];     // every value that IS present cancels with its twin index
int present = 6;                        // 0000 0110 — a value that DOES appear in nums
int doubled = present << 1;             // shift left  -> multiply by 2
int halved  = present >> 1;             // shift right -> divide by 2
int isOdd   = present & 1;              // keep the lowest bit only
int dropped = present & (present - 1);  // clear the lowest set bit
int lowest  = present & -present;       // isolate the lowest set bit
int gone    = present ^ present;        // <-- a ^ a == 0: this is why every present value cancels

commonMistakes: Seeding the XOR with 0 instead of n: the index n is then never folded in, and the result is the true answer XORed with n — so [0,1] returns 0 instead of 2, and [3,0,1] returns 1 instead of 2. The failing case is any input, but the one people notice is when the missing value is n itself and the method returns 0.

Using n * (n + 1) / 2 - sum with an int accumulator: past roughly n = 65,000 the total exceeds 2^31 and wraps, so the method is right on every small test and returns a negative or nonsensical index on the large one. Either use long, or use XOR, whose intermediate values never grow.

Marking presence in a boolean[] of size n rather than n + 1 and indexing seen[nums[i]] — the first input that actually contains the value n throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, which is exactly the [0,1] case.

practice.note: LeetCode 268 uses the range 0..n; this lesson also covers the 1..n variant, where the sum formula shifts by n but the XOR approach is unchanged.
